usage: attaches the time particle 에 for 'during the AM'
period word comes BEFORE the clock time
오전 directly modifies the following noun, no 의
내내 stresses the whole stretch of the AM
examples: 오전에 회의가 있어요.
I have a meeting in the morning.
basic: 에 marks the time-when
저는 보통 오전 열 시에 일어나요.
I usually get up at 10 AM.
everyday: period 오전 + hour 열 시 + 에 together
오전 중으로 연락드릴게요.
I'll get in touch sometime during the morning.
real-situation: 오전 중(으로) = 'within the AM', polite work register
nuance: 오전 is the Sino-Korean clock label for the AM half of the day, literally 午前 'before noon' (午 = noon, 前 = before), and its mirror is 오후 午後 'after noon'. The key contrast learners blur is 오전 vs 아침: 아침 is the FELT early part of the day (sunrise to mid-morning, and also breakfast), while 오전 is the neutral clock span from midnight-ish to 12:00 used on schedules, tickets, and timetables. So you say 아침에 커피를 마셔요 (lived experience) but 오전 9시 출발 (a printed departure). It is more formal/factual than 아침 and pairs habitually with clock times (오전 9시), 회의/수업/근무, and 오전 중. The classic English-speaker pitfall is word order: AM attaches AFTER the number in English ('9 AM'), but in Korean the period leads, so it must be 오전 9시, never 9시 오전. Also do not reach for 오전 when you simply mean the breakfast-time feel of 'morning' — use 아침.

Putting the period after the hour, e.g. 아홉 시 오전 — Korean fixes the order as 오전 아홉 시 (period first, then clock time).
Dropping 에 in 오전 회의 있어요 — to mark 'during the morning' you need 오전에 회의가 있어요.

usage: day word + 오후 stack with no particle between
examples: 오후에 친구를 만나요.
I meet a friend in the afternoon.
basic: 에 marks time-when
오후 두 시에 약속이 있어요.
I have an appointment at 2 PM.
everyday: 오후 + 두 시 + 에 in sequence
오후 늦게 비가 올 것 같아요.
It looks like it'll rain late in the afternoon.
real-situation: 오후 늦게 = 'late in the PM', a fixed phrase
nuance: 오후 is the Sino-Korean PM label, literally 午後 'after noon' (午 noon, 後 after), the exact counterpart of 오전 午前. It covers every PM hour from 12:00 until evening, where it hands off to 저녁. The contrast to watch is 오후 vs 저녁: 오후 is the neutral clock-PM you write on schedules (오후 3시 회의), while 저녁 is the lived early-evening AND the dinner meal; so a 6 p.m. plan can be 오후 6시 on a timetable but 저녁 when you talk about eating. 오후 collocates with clock times (오후 3시), 수업/회의/근무, and the fixed 오후 늦게 'late in the afternoon'. The number-one English-speaker pitfall is order: 'PM' follows the number in English but the period LEADS in Korean — say 오후 5시, never 5시 오후. A second trap is treating 오후 as a greeting-time word like 'good afternoon'; Korean has no clock-based greeting, so you still say 안녕하세요, not anything built on 오후.

Using 오후 for an early-evening dinner plan — for the dinner-time feel switch to 저녁 (저녁 여섯 시), since 오후 is the neutral daytime-PM span.

usage: time + 에 for the time-when reading
here 아침 is the meal, so it takes object 을
아침 + adverb 일찍, a set collocation
examples: 아침에 커피를 마셔요.
I drink coffee in the morning.
basic: 아침에 = the time slot
저는 아침을 안 먹어요.
I don't eat breakfast.
everyday: 아침 + 을 shows it's the MEAL, object of 먹다
아침 일찍 출발하면 길이 안 막혀요.
If we leave early in the morning, traffic won't be jammed.
real-situation: 아침 일찍 set phrase + conditional 면
nuance: 아침 is a native Korean word that does double duty: the early part of the day (roughly sunrise to mid-morning) and the breakfast meal — the same way English 'morning' differs from the meal but Korean merges the breakfast sense into the time word. The grammar disambiguates: with 에 (아침에) it's the time, with 을 (아침을 먹다) it's the food. Contrast 아침 vs 오전: 아침 is the felt, lived early morning, while 오전 午前 is the neutral clock-AM you put on timetables — so 아침에 일어나요 (waking life) but 오전 9시 회의 (a scheduled item). Habitual partners: 아침에 일어나다/운동하다, 아침을 먹다/거르다 ('skip breakfast'), 아침 일찍, 매일 아침. The big English-speaker pitfall is using 오전 for the breakfast meal — 오전 is only the clock period and can never name food, so 'eat breakfast' must be 아침을 먹다, never 오전을 먹다. Also don't force 에 onto the meal sense: you eat 아침을, you don't 'eat at morning'.

examples: 점심 같이 먹어요.
Let's have lunch together.
basic: object 을 is often dropped in casual speech → just 점심 먹다
점심에 뭐 먹을 거예요?
What are you going to eat for lunch?
everyday: 점심에 = the time slot + future 을 거예요
점심 먹었어요?
Have you eaten lunch (yet)?
real-situation: a routine greeting that means 'how are you', not a literal question
nuance: 점심 is Sino-Korean, literally 點心 — 點 'a dot/spot' + 心 'heart/center', an old phrase for a small 'touch-the-heart' midday bite that came to mean both the noon-time and the lunch meal. Like 아침/저녁, grammar splits the senses: 점심을 먹다 (the meal) vs 점심에 (the time). Note the near-synonym 정오 正午 'exactly noon' is the precise clock point 12:00, while 점심 is the looser lunch-time/meal — you'd never say 정오를 먹다. Habitual partners: 점심을 먹다, 점심시간, 점심 약속, 점심 메뉴, and the ritual greeting 점심 먹었어요?. Two English-speaker pitfalls: (1) translating 'lunch break' word-for-word — Korean uses the set compound 점심시간, not 점심 휴식; (2) reading 점심 먹었어요? literally and giving a detailed menu report — like 'how's it going', it's mostly phatic, and 네, 먹었어요 is enough. Also remember the meal is an object (점심을 먹다), so don't say 점심에 먹다 when you mean eating the lunch itself.

usage: 식사 'a meal' makes the dinner sense explicit & polite
day word + 저녁 with no particle between
examples: 저녁에 영화를 봐요.
I watch a movie in the evening.
basic: 저녁에 = the time slot
저녁 뭐 먹을까요?
What should we eat for dinner?
everyday: meal 을 dropped in casual speech + 을까요 suggestion
오늘 저녁에 시간 괜찮으면 같이 식사해요.
If you're free this evening, let's eat together.
real-situation: 저녁에 (time) + polite invitation 식사하다
nuance: 저녁 is a native Korean word covering the early-night period AND the dinner meal, mirroring 아침/점심: 저녁을 먹다 is the food, 저녁에 is the time. The fine line is 저녁 vs 밤: 저녁 is the social early evening — dusk through dinner, when people are still out — whereas 밤 is true late night when it's dark and quiet; so a 7 p.m. dinner is 저녁, but 11 p.m. is 밤. 저녁 also contrasts with the clock label 오후, which ends as 저녁 begins. Habitual partners: 저녁을 먹다, 저녁 식사, 저녁 약속, 저녁 메뉴, 저녁에 만나다. The main English-speaker pitfall is using 밤 for the dinner meal because 'night' feels close — but 'eat dinner' is 저녁을 먹다, never 밤을 먹다 (밤 can't name a meal, and 밤 also happens to mean 'chestnut'). A second trap: don't mark the dinner-meal with 에; you eat 저녁을, while 저녁에 means 'in the evening (do something)'.

Using 저녁 for genuinely late night (e.g. midnight) — past dinner into the dark, quiet hours it becomes 밤; 저녁 is the early, social evening.
Marking the meal with 에 (저녁에 먹어요, meaning the food) — the dinner-as-object needs 을: 저녁을 먹어요.

usage: compound; note the inserted ㅅ (사이시옷): 어제+밤
examples: 밤에 책을 읽어요.
I read books at night.
basic: 밤에 = the time slot
밤늦게까지 일했어요.
I worked until late at night.
everyday: set adverb 밤늦게 + 까지 'until'
어젯밤에 잠을 잘 못 잤어요.
I couldn't sleep well last night.
real-situation: 어젯밤 (note 사이시옷) + 잘 못 자다 'can't sleep well'
nuance: 밤 is a native word for true night — the dark, quiet hours after 저녁, peaking around bedtime and past midnight. The contrast to fix is 밤 vs 저녁: 저녁 is the social early evening (dusk to dinner) while 밤 is deep night, so 7 p.m. is 저녁 but 11 p.m. or 1 a.m. is 밤. A spelling point: 'last night' is 어젯밤 with an inserted ㅅ (사이시옷) and is preferred over the looser 어제 밤; 'tomorrow night' is 내일 밤. Habitual partners: 밤에 자다, 밤늦게, 밤새(우다) 'stay up all night', 어젯밤, 깊은 밤 'the dead of night'. The English-speaker pitfall: 밤 only names the time of night and can NEVER mean the dinner meal — that's 저녁; and beware the homograph 밤 also means 'chestnut', so context (밤에 vs 밤을 굽다 'roast chestnuts') keeps them apart. Finally, like other pure time words 밤 takes 에 for 'at night' (밤에), so don't drop it when stating when something happens.

examples: 오늘 무슨 요일이에요?
What day of the week is it today?
basic: the standard way to ask the weekday
수업이 무슨 요일에 있어요?
What day of the week is the class on?
everyday: 무슨 요일 + 에 to ask the time-when
요일마다 운동 종목을 바꿔요.
I switch the workout by the day of the week.
real-situation: 요일마다 = 'each day-of-week', a habitual pattern
nuance: 요일 is the Sino-Korean suffix that builds weekday names, 曜日 — 曜 'celestial body/light' + 日 'day', the same East-Asian system that names days after the sun, moon, and five elements: 일(日)요일 Sun, 월(月)요일 Moon, 화(火)요일 Fire/Mars, 수(水)요일 Water, 목(木)요일 Wood, 금(金)요일 Metal/Gold, 토(土)요일 Earth. By itself 요일 means 'day of the week' as a category. The key usage point is the question word: to ask which weekday you MUST use 무슨 요일이에요?, because 무슨 asks 'what kind/which of a known set'; 어느 요일 or 어떤 요일 sound unnatural here. Habitual partners: 무슨 요일, 요일마다, 요일별, 주말/평일 요일. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'which day → 어느', producing 어느 요일이에요?; Korean idiom locks this to 무슨 요일. Also, when you name a specific day for scheduling, the time particle is 에 (월요일에 가요), and 요일 stays attached to its element (no space inside 월요일).

Splitting the word, e.g. 월 요일 — each weekday is one closed word: 월요일, 화요일, …

usage: time + 에 (not 에서) for the time-when
examples: 주말에 보통 쉬어요.
I usually rest on the weekend.
basic: 주말에 marks the time-when
이번 주말에 뭐 해요?
What are you doing this weekend?
everyday: 이번 주말 + 에 + casual plan question
주말 잘 보내세요!
Have a good weekend!
real-situation: set parting phrase coworkers say on Friday
nuance: 주말 is Sino-Korean, 週末 — 週 'week' + 末 'end', literally 'week-end', and its opposites are 평일 平日 'weekday' and 주중 週中 'midweek'. It refers to Saturday and Sunday as a block. The contrast worth noting is 주말 vs 휴일: 주말 is specifically the weekend, while 휴일 休日 is any day off including public holidays — so a Wednesday holiday is a 휴일 but not a 주말. Habitual partners: 주말에 쉬다/놀다, 이번/지난/다음 주말, 주말마다, 즐거운 주말, and the farewell 주말 잘 보내세요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: learners borrow 'at/on' loosely and write 주말에서, but 에서 marks a LOCATION or a source ('from'); the time-when always takes 에 → 주말에. A second subtlety: for 'this weekend' use 이번 주말 (이번 = the current instance), not 오늘 주말; and 다음 주말 'next weekend' vs 다음 주 주말 can differ, so keep 다음 주말 for the upcoming Sat–Sun.

The contrast worth noting is 주말 vs 휴일: 주말 is specifically the weekend, while 휴일 休日 is any day off including public holidays — so a Wednesday holiday is a 휴일 but not a 주말.
주말 is Sino-Korean, 週末 — 週 'week' + 末 'end', literally 'week-end'.

The pitfall is the particle: learners borrow 'at/on' loosely and write 주말에서, but 에서 marks a LOCATION or a source ('from'); the time-when always takes 에 → 주말에. mistakes: Writing 주말에서 for 'on the weekend' — 에서 is for place/source; the time-when is 주말에.
Saying 오늘 주말 for 'this weekend' — use 이번 주말 (이번 marks the current weekend); 오늘 주말 mixes 'today' with 'weekend'.
Treating any day off as 주말 — a midweek public holiday is a 휴일, not a 주말 (which is strictly Sat–Sun).

usage: bare time word, normally NO 에
the other day / a couple days ago
examples: 어제 친구를 만났어요.
I met a friend yesterday.
basic: bare 어제 + past tense, no 에
어제부터 목이 좀 아파요.
My throat has been a bit sore since yesterday.
everyday: 어제부터 'since yesterday' + ongoing state
어제 본 영화 정말 재미있었어요.
The movie I watched yesterday was really fun.
real-situation: 어제 modifying a past clause (본) + past evaluation
nuance: 어제 is a native deictic time word meaning 'yesterday', sitting in the set 그저께(엊그제) 'day before yesterday' – 어제 – 오늘 'today' – 내일 'tomorrow' – 모레 'day after tomorrow'. Its defining grammar quirk is that, like 오늘 and 내일, it normally takes NO 에: you say 어제 만났어요, never 어제에. (The particle reappears only when 어제 combines with a sub-period, e.g. 어제 아침에, where 에 attaches to 아침.) 어제 naturally pairs with past tense — 았어요/었어요 — so it's a reliable signal that the verb should be past. Habitual partners: 어제 아침/저녁, 어제부터, 어제 일 'yesterday's matter', 어제 본/한/간 + noun. The big English-speaker pitfall is over-marking with 에 by analogy to 'on' or to other time nouns like 주말에; bare 어제 is correct. A second trap is pairing 어제 with present or future tense; because it's firmly past, 어제 가요 is wrong — it must be 어제 갔어요.

examples: 사과 세 개 주세요.
Three apples, please.
basic: noun–number–counter, object 를 often dropped when ordering
이거 한 개에 얼마예요?
How much is this per one?
everyday: 한 개에 = 'per item', price-per-unit 에
라면 몇 개 남았어요?
How many packs of ramyeon are left?
real-situation: 몇 개 asking quantity + 남다 'be left'
nuance: 개 is the Sino-Korean general counter for inanimate objects, 個/箇, the catch-all you use when no more specific counter fits (it won't do for people, animals, or flat/long things, which have their own counters). It REQUIRES native Korean numbers, and the first four plus 20 shorten before any counter: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무 (so 한 개, 두 개, 세 개, 네 개, 스무 개). Word order is fixed as noun + number + 개 (사과 세 개), unlike English 'three apples'. Habitual partners: 한 개에 (price per item), 몇 개, 여러 개 'several', 개수 'the count'. The headline English-speaker pitfall is using Sino numbers with 개 — 일 개, 이 개 is wrong; counters like 개/명/마리 take native numbers (한 개), even though money/minutes take Sino. A second trap is English order: don't say 세 사과 개 or 개 세 사과; it's 사과 세 개. Note the contrast with 명/분 (people) and 마리 (animals): 개 is strictly for things.

examples: 학생이 다섯 명 있어요.
There are five students.
basic: subject 이 on the noun, count after it
몇 명이세요?
How many (people) are you? / For how many?
everyday: a server's set phrase at a restaurant
회의에 다섯 분이 오셨어요.
Five people (honored) came to the meeting.
real-situation: honorific 분 + 오시다 replaces 명 for respected guests
nuance: 명 is the Sino-Korean counter for people, 名 'name/person', and like all counters it takes native numbers: 한 명, 두 명, 세 명 (with the usual shortening 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무). The crucial register contrast is 명 vs 분: 분 is the honorific people-counter for guests, elders, customers, or anyone you respect, so a waiter asks 몇 분이세요? and you describe esteemed visitors as 세 분이 오셨어요, while 명 is the plain, neutral count fine for friends, students, or stating numbers factually (학생 세 명). Using 명 for a venerable elder can sound curt; using 분 for yourself sounds odd. Habitual partners: 몇 명/몇 분, 한 명도 없다 'not a single person', 인원 'headcount'. The top English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the all-purpose 개 to count people — 개 is for things only; people must be 명 (or honorific 분), never 사람 세 개. A second trap is Sino numbers (이 명); counters take native (두 명).

examples: 이거 얼마예요? — 삼천 원이에요.
How much is this? — It's 3,000 won.
basic: 얼마예요 question + Sino price answer
전부 만 오천 원입니다.
That's 15,000 won in total.
everyday: 만 오천 = 10,000+5,000, polite 입니다 at a register
카드로 삼만 원 결제할게요.
I'll pay 30,000 won by card.
real-situation: 삼만 = 30,000 + 카드로 'by card' + 결제하다
nuance: 원 is the Korean currency unit (the symbol is ₩) and, like all money and clock-number words, it REQUIRES Sino-Korean numbers: 일·이·삼·사·오·육·칠·팔·구·십·백·천·만 (so 천 원, 만 원, 오천 원). The single biggest stumbling block for English speakers is the 만 'ten-thousand' place: Korean groups large numbers by 10,000, not 1,000, so 만 원 = 10,000 won (not 1,000), 십만 = 100,000, 백만 = 1,000,000. Reading prices therefore means re-chunking — 30,000 is 삼만 (3×10,000), 15,000 is 만 오천. Habitual partners: 얼마예요?, 만 원짜리 'a 10,000-won bill/item', ~원만 'just ~won', 거스름돈 'change'. The headline pitfall, beyond the comma-grouping, is using NATIVE numbers with 원 (한 원, 두 원) — money never takes native numbers; it's 천 원, 만 원. Contrast this with counters like 개/명, which take native numbers — Korean splits the two systems, and 원 firmly sits on the Sino side. Also note 원 is read after the full number, e.g. 사천오백 원, with no 'and'.
